introduction: “Thy heart is My home; sanctify it for My descent.” The guide’s subject is the inmost heart, which the Báb’s writings call fu’ád and set above intellect: a balance that never strays, an eye that can see what reasoning cannot, a tablet to be written on, a throne. The Bible speaks this language constantly. The pure in heart shall see God; a clean heart is asked for and a new heart promised; the law is to be written within; the kingdom is within; the Father and the Son will make their abode. Pascal gave the West its sentence about the heart’s reasons, Plotinus and Mencius their inward turn. The difficulty is Jeremiah’s: “The heart is deceitful above all things.” Plato would not trust the soul to anything but reason’s hand on the reins, and Aristotle finds the mean by practical wisdom.
questions: Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful; reading 1 calls the inmost heart a balance that never strays. Are they speaking of the same thing? What in the readings separates the two (see 5 and 9)?
“Thy heart is My home.” What do the companions from John and the Apocalypse add about who acts first, the guest or the host?
Pascal says the heart has reasons unknown to reason; Plato says reason must hold the reins. What exactly do readings 18 and 19 claim the heart can do that intellect cannot?
The reading says Paul knew everything before and nothing after. What kind of unknowing is this, and how is it different from ignorance?

outside.why: The true balance that never strays “is the balance of the inmost heart”. Pascal: the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
Jeremiah: the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? I the Lord search the heart. Which heart is a balance that never strays, and which is this one?
“Thy heart is My home; sanctify it for My descent.” If a man love me, my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.
Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him.
He cannot express the fellowship realized in the heart. Paul heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.

Paul, the reading says, knew everything before Christ and nothing after. His own words: what things were gain to me, those I counted loss; I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ.
Socrates found his one advantage in the same place: I neither know nor think that I know.
“Purify the heart … from all contingent things.” Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
The beatitude names what a purified heart is for: blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
The faculty of the heart is the greatest of gifts. Ezekiel’s promise is of a heart given: a new heart also will I give you, and I will take away the stony heart.
The inmost heart as a treasury. Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
Seven stages, from the mineral upward. Rumi: I died as mineral and became a plant, I died as plant and rose to animal, I died as animal and I was man.
“Were they to open the eye of the heart.” The Qur’an: it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts, which are within the bosoms, that grow blind.
Healing comes through “the condition of the heart”. A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Write it “with the ink of light upon the tablet of thy spirit”. Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men.
I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.
The station of those who have attained is “the throne of the inmost heart”. The kingdom of God is within you.
Plotinus’s counsel to one who would see the beautiful: withdraw into yourself and look.
The heart is the highest stage of a created being’s existence. Mencius: the great end of learning is nothing else but to seek for the lost heart.

Truth is revealed “through the gaze of the heart, and not that of intellect”. Plato gives the reins to reason: the charioteer must master the horses or the soul never rises. What do the readings fear from the intellect, and Plato from what is not intellect?

The Middle Path between two extremes “can be comprehended by naught save the heart”. Aristotle also places virtue in a mean, and says it is determined by reason, as the man of practical wisdom would determine it. Is his practical wisdom so far from the reading’s heart?
